source_text: 1. Verum quoniam de tantis et talibus rebus disserentibus non suffieit humanis sensibus et communi intellectui summam rei committere et, ut ita dixerim, visibiliter de invisibilibus pronuntiare, assumenda sunt nobis ad probationem horum, quae dicimus, etiam divinarum scripturarum testimonia. Quae testimonia ut certam et indubitatam "tree d o habeant fidem sive in his, quae dicenda a nobis, sive quae iam dicta sunt, necessarium prius videtur ostendere quod ipsae scripturae divinae sint, id est dei spiritu inspiratae. lgitur quam poterimus breviter etiam de hoc adsignabimus ex ipsis divinis scripturis quae nos conpetenter moverint proferentes, id est de Moyseo primo, legislatore gentis Hebraeae, et ex verbis lesu Christi, auctoris et principis Christianorum religionis et dogmatis. Cum enim permulti legislatores extiterint apud Graecos et barbaros, innumeri quoque doctores vel philosophi veritatem se pollicentes adserere, nullum meminimus legislatorem adfectum quendam et studium etiam exterarum gentium animis inicere potuisse, ut leges suas vel susciperent libenter vel cum omni animi intentione defenderent. Nemo ergo eam quae sibi visa est veritatem non solum pluribus aliis exteris nationibus, ‚sed ne uni quidem genti ita insinuare atque inolescere potuit, ut ad omnes eius scientia vel credulitas perveniret. Et quidem dubitari non potest quod et legislatores optaverint observari ab omnibus, si fieri posset, hominibus leges suas, et magistri, omnibus innotescere eam quae sibi visa fuerat veritatem. Sed scientes quia id omnino non possent, nee virtus in eis aliqua tanta subsisteret, quae etiam exteras nationes ad legum suarum vel adsertionum observantiam provocaret, ne conari quidem hoc aut incipere omnino ausi sunt, ne inprudentes eos etiam in hoc inefficax et inexplebile notaret inceptum. At vero in omni orbe terrarum, in omni Graecia atque universis exteris nationibus innumeri sunt et inmensi, qui relictis patris legibus et his, quos putabant deos, ad observantiam Moysi legis et discipulatum se Christi ceultumque tradiderunt, et hoc non sine ingenti odio adversum se commoto eorum, qui simulacra venerantur, ita ut ab his frequenter et cruciatibus adfligantur, nonnumquam etiam agantur in mortem; amplectuntur tamen et cum omni affectu custodiunt doctrinae Christi sermonem. Et est videre quomodo brevi tempore ipsa religio creverit, poenis eultorum mortibusque proficiens, sed et bonorum direptionibus atque omni ab his suppliciorum genere tolerato; et eo maxime mirum est quod ne doctores quidem ipsi vel satis idonei sunt vel satis plures: “praedicatur’ tamen sermo iste -in omni orbe terrarum”, ita ut ‘Graeci ac barbari, sapientes et insipientes’ religionem Christianae doctrinae suscipiant. Ex quo dubium non est “non haec humanis’ viribus aut ‘opibus” agi, ut cum omni potestate et creduhtate sermo Christi lesu apud omnium mentes atque animos convalescat. Nam et praedicta esse ab eo haec ipsa et divinis ab eo responsis confirmata, manifestum est cum dicit quia “apud praesides et iudices adducemini propter me, in testimonium ipsis et gentibuse; et rursum: “Praedieabitur hoe evangelium in omnibus gentibus”; et iterum: “Multi mihi dicent in illa die: Domine, domine, nonne in tuo nomine mandueavimus et bibimus, et in tuo nomine daemonia eiecimus? et dicam eis: Discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis s numquam cognovi vosc”. Quae si ita quidem dicta ab eo fuissent nee tamen ad finem ea, quae praedicta sunt, pervenissent, fortassis minus esse vera viderentur nec habere aliquid auctoritatis. Nune vero cum in effectum res, quae fuerant ab eo praedictae, perveniant, cum tanta autem potestate atque auctoritate praedictae sint, manifestissime declaratur deum vere esse, qui homo factus salutaria praecepta hominibus tradidit. 3. Quid vero inde dicendum est quod prophetae de ipso antea praedixerant ‘non cessaturos principes ex luda neque duces ex femoribus eius, usquequo veniat ille, cui repositum este regnum scilicet, et "usquequo veniat expectatio gentium-? Manifestissime enim ex ipsa bistoria apparet et ex his, quae hodie pervidentur, quia ex temporibus Christi ultra reges apud ludaeos non extiterunt. Sed et omnes illae ambitiones Iudaicae, in quibus iactantiae quam plurimum gerebant et in quibus exultabant, id est vel de templi decore vel de altaris insignibus atque omnibus illis sacerdotalibus infulis indumentisque pontificum, simul universa destructa sunt. Completa est enim prophetia, quae dixerat: “Per dies multos sedebunt fili Israhel sine rege, sine principe; non erit hostia nec altare nec sacerdotium nec responsa”. His ergo testimonis utimur adversum eos, qui videntur adse rere de his, quae in Genesi ab lacob dicta sunt, quod de luda dieta sint et dicunt permanere adhue principem ex genere ludae, istum videlicet, qui est gentis ipsorum princeps, quem nominant patriarcham, nec deficere posse de semine eius qui permaneant usque ad adventum eius Christi, quem sibi ipsi describunt. Sed si verum est quod ait propheta, quia “dies multos sedebunt fili Israhel sine rege, sine principe; nec erit hostia nec altare nec sacerdotium”, et utique ex quo subversum est templum -nec hostiae- offeruntur “nec altare- invenitur “nec sacerdotiumconstat: certissimum est defecisse “principes ex luda-, sieut scriptum est, et -ducem ex femoribus eius, usquequo venit ille, eui repositum est Constat ergo quia ‘venit ille, cui repositum este, in quo et ‘expectatio gentium- est. Quod manifeste videtur impletum de multitudine eorum, qui per Christum deo ex diversis gentibus crediderunt. 4. Sed et in Deuteronomii cantico per prophetiam designatur pro peccatis prioris populi futura esse insensatae gentis electio, non alia utique quam haec, quae per Christum facta est. Sie enim ait: “Exacerbaverunt me in simulacris suis, et ego in zelo concitabo eos, in gente insipiente inritabo eos”. Est ergo satis evidenter agnoscere, quemammodum Hebraei, qui deum ‘exacerbasse’ dieuntur in his, qui non sunt du, et inritasse eum ‘in simulacris suis. inritati sunt et ipsi in zelotypia per ‘gentem insipientem”, quam deus -elegit- per adventum Christi lesu et discipulos eius. Sie enim dicit apostolus: “Videte enim vocationem vestram, fratres, quoniam non multi sapientes inter vos secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles; sed quae stulta sunt mundi elegit deus et ea, quae non sunt, ut ea, quae erant prius, destrueret”. Non ergo ‘glorietur- ‘carnalis Israhel-;
pass_a_gloss: But since for discussing such great and important matters it is not enough for human senses and common understanding to commit the sum of the matter and, so to speak, visibly pronounce about invisible things, we must also take up for proof of what we say the testimonies of divine scriptures. Which testimonies, so that they may have certain and undoubted faith, whether in those things that must be said by us or in those things that have already been said, it seems necessary first to show that the divine scriptures themselves are inspired by the Spirit of God. Therefore, as briefly as possible, we will also assign to this from the divine scriptures themselves, which have moved us competently, bringing forth, that is, from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and prince of the Christian religion and doctrine. For when many lawgivers have existed among the Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable doctors or philosophers have promised to assert the truth, we do not recall any lawgiver who could have inspired a certain affection and study even in the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either willingly receive his laws or defend them with all intention of their mind. No one, therefore, could have insinuated the truth that seemed to him, not only to many other foreign nations, but not even to one nation, so that their knowledge or belief would reach all. And indeed, it cannot be doubted that lawgivers have wished their laws to be observed by all men, if it could be done, and masters, that the truth that seemed to them would become known to all. But knowing that they could not do this at all, nor did any such great virtue exist in them, which could also provoke foreign nations to the observance of their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to try this or begin it, lest they be noted as imprudent and ineffective in this undertaking. But in the whole world, in all of Greece, and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and immense numbers who, having abandoned the laws of their fathers and the gods they thought were gods, have given themselves to the observance of Moses' law and the discipleship of Christ, and this not without great hatred having been stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are often afflicted by torments and sometimes even led to death; yet they embrace and guard with all affection the doctrine of Christ's word. And it is evident how in a short time the religion itself has grown, profiting from the punishments and deaths of its cultivators, and also from the plundering of goods and every kind of suffering endured by them; and it is all the more wonderful that not even the doctors themselves are sufficient or numerous enough: 'this word is preached in the whole world', so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish' receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From which it is not doubtful that 'these things are not done by human strength or resources', so that with all power and credibility the word of Christ Jesus may prevail in the minds and souls of all. For it is evident that these things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says that 'you will be led before princes and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations'; and again: 'This gospel will be preached in all nations'; and again: 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I never knew you'. If these things had been said by him, but had not come to pass, perhaps they would seem less true and would not have any authority. But now, since the things that were predicted by him have come to pass, and have been predicted with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists, who, having become man, handed down salutary precepts to men. But what must be said about the fact that the prophets predicted beforehand that 'the princes will not cease from Judah, nor the leaders from his thighs, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been entrusted, and until the expectation of the nations comes'? For it is most evident from history itself and from what is seen today that from the times of Christ, there have been no kings among the Jews. But also all those Jewish ambitions, in which they carried on much boasting and exultation, that is, either about the decoration of the temple or the insignia of the altar and all those priestly robes and vestments of the pontiffs, have been completely destroyed. For the prophecy has been fulfilled, which said: 'For many days the sons of Israel will sit without a king, without a prince; there will be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood, no responses'. We use these testimonies against those who seem to assert that the things said by Jacob in Genesis about Judah remain to this day, that the prince from the tribe of Judah has not failed, but rather that he who is the prince of their nation, whom they call the patriarch, remains, and that those from his seed will remain until the coming of Christ, whom they describe for themselves. But if it is true what the prophet says, that 'the sons of Israel will sit for many days without a king, without a prince; there will be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood', and indeed, since the temple has been overthrown, no sacrifices are offered, no altar is found, no priesthood exists, it is most certain that the princes from Judah have failed, as it is written, and the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been entrusted. Therefore, it is established that 'he has come to whom the kingdom has been entrusted', in whom also 'the expectation of the nations' is. Which is clearly seen to be fulfilled in the multitude of those who have believed in God through Christ from diverse nations. But also in the song of Deuteronomy, it is designated through prophecy that there will be an election of a foolish nation for the sins of the previous people, not another, certainly, than this one that has been made through Christ. For thus it says: 'They have provoked me with their idols, and I will provoke them with a foolish nation'. Therefore, it is sufficiently evident to recognize how the Hebrews, who are said to have provoked God with their idols, and to have provoked him with their idols, have been provoked themselves in zeal through the 'foolish nation', which God has chosen through the coming of Christ Jesus and his disciples. For thus the apostle says: 'See your calling, brothers, that not many wise men are among you according to the flesh, not many powerful men, not many noble men; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world and the things that are not, that he may destroy the things that were'. Therefore, 'fleshly Israel' does not glory; for the apostle says: 'See your calling, brothers, that not many wise men are among you according to the flesh, not many powerful men, not many noble men; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world and the things that are not'
pass_b_english: But since, when discussing matters so great and of such a kind, it is not enough for human senses and common understanding to entrust the sum of the matter and, so to speak, to pronounce visibly about invisible things, we must also take up the testimonies of the divine scriptures as proof of what we say. So that these testimonies may have a certain and undoubted faith — whether in the things that must be said by us or in those already said — it seems necessary first to show that the scriptures themselves are divine, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. Therefore, as briefly as we can, we will also set down on this point from the divine scriptures themselves, which have moved us competently, bringing them forward: that is, from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew nation, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and prince of the Christian religion and doctrine. For when many lawgivers had existed among the Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable teachers or philosophers had promised to assert the truth, we do not recall that any lawgiver was able to inspire a certain affection and zeal even in the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either receive his laws willingly or defend them with all their mind's intent. No one, therefore, was able to insinuate the truth that seemed right to him, not only into many other foreign nations, but not even into a single nation, so that their knowledge or belief would reach everyone. And indeed, it cannot be doubted that the lawgivers wished their laws to be observed by all men, if it could be done, and the masters, that the truth that seemed right to them would become known to all. But knowing that they could not do this at all, nor did any such great virtue exist in them that could also provoke foreign nations to the observance of their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to attempt this or to begin it at all, lest they be marked as imprudent and ineffective in this undertaking. But in the whole world, in all Greece, and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and immense numbers who, having abandoned the laws of their fathers and those whom they thought were gods, have given themselves over to the observance of Moses' law and to the discipleship and cultivation of Christ. And this not without great hatred having been stirred up against them by those who venerate images, so that they are often afflicted with torments, and sometimes even led to death; yet they embrace and guard with all affection the word of Christ's doctrine. And it is evident how in a short time the religion itself has grown, advancing through the penalties and deaths of its cultivators, and also through the plundering of goods and every kind of punishment endured by them. And it is all the more wonderful that not even the teachers themselves are either sufficiently suitable or sufficiently numerous: 'this word is preached in the whole world' (Matt 24:14), so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish' (Rom 1:14) receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From which there is no doubt that 'these things are not done by human strength or resources', so that with all power and credibility the word of Christ Jesus may prevail in the minds and souls of all. For it is evident that these very things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says that 'you will be led before governors and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations' (Matt 10:18); and again: 'This gospel will be preached in all nations' (Matt 24:14); and again: 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not eat and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I never knew you' (Matt 7:22-23). If these things had been said by him, but had not come to pass, perhaps they would seem less true and would not have any authority. But now, since the things that were predicted by him have come to pass, and have been predicted with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists, who, having become man, handed down salutary precepts to men.

But what must be said about the fact that the prophets predicted beforehand concerning him that 'the princes will not cease from Judah, nor the leaders from his thighs, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been entrusted, and until the expectation of the nations comes' (Gen 49:10)? For it is most evident from history itself and from what is seen today that from the times of Christ, there have been no kings among the Jews. But also all those Jewish ambitions, in which they carried on much boasting and in which they exulted — that is, either about the decoration of the temple or the insignia of the altar and all those priestly robes and vestments of the high priests — have been completely destroyed. For the prophecy has been fulfilled, which said: 'For many days the sons of Israel will sit without a king, without a prince; there will be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood, no responses' (Hos 3:4). We use these testimonies against those who seem to assert that the things said by Jacob in Genesis about Judah remain to this day, that the prince from the tribe of Judah has not failed, but rather that he who is the prince of their nation, whom they call the patriarch, remains, and that those from his seed will remain until the coming of Christ, whom they describe for themselves. But if it is true what the prophet says, that 'the sons of Israel will sit for many days without a king, without a prince; there will be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood', and indeed, since the temple has been overthrown, no sacrifices are offered, no altar is found, no priesthood exists, it is most certain that the princes from Judah have failed, as it is written, and the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been entrusted. Therefore, it is established that 'he has come to whom the kingdom has been entrusted', in whom also 'the expectation of the nations' is. Which is clearly seen to be fulfilled in the multitude of those who have believed in God through Christ from diverse nations.

But also in the song of Deuteronomy, it is designated through prophecy that there will be an election of a foolish nation for the sins of the previous people, not another, certainly, than this one that has been made through Christ. For thus it says: 'They have provoked me with their idols, and I will provoke them with a foolish nation' (Deut 32:21). Therefore, it is sufficiently evident to recognize how the Hebrews, who are said to have provoked God with their idols, and to have provoked him with their idols, have been provoked themselves in zeal through the 'foolish nation', which God has chosen through the coming of Christ Jesus and his disciples. For thus the apostle says: 'See your calling, brothers, that not many wise men are among you according to the flesh, not many powerful men, not many noble men; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world and the things that are not, that he may destroy the things that were' (1 Cor 1:26-28). Therefore, 'fleshly Israel' does not glory; for the apostle says: 'See your calling, brothers, that not many wise men are among you according to the flesh, not many powerful men, not many noble men; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world and the things that are not, that he may destroy the things that were' (1 Cor 1:26-28).
